idiom_name: enum OrderEvent + trait EventHandler<E> registered by TypeId
implementation_notes: The canonical Rust shape is a plain enum for the closed event set (OrderEvent::Placed { order_id, occurred_on }) with match for exhaustive handling, plus a trait for the reaction (trait EventHandler<E> { fn handle(&self, e: &E); }) and an explicit registry when handlers are registered at runtime - typically a HashMap<TypeId, Vec<Box<dyn Any>>> with downcasting or a typed registration API. No inheritance means the enum replaces the base-class hierarchy, and ownership means the event is moved or borrowed explicitly, so handlers state whether they may consume it.
pitfalls: TypeId/Any registries downcast at dispatch time: a handler registered for the wrong type compiles and is silently never called.
A closed enum forces every dispatcher to recompile when an event is added; trait objects keep the set open but lose exhaustive matching - pick one model and apply it consistently.

variants.name: Tokio broadcast channel fan-out
variants.implementation_notes: When reactions are asynchronous tasks rather than in-transaction functions, the bus is a broadcast channel: broadcast::channel(capacity) returns a Sender whose subscribe() gives each consumer its own Receiver, every sent value is cloned to all consumers, and a lagging receiver observes RecvError::Lagged instead of stalling the producer. Events stay plain structs or enums; what changes is that the dispatcher is a bounded runtime queue and handlers are tasks, so dispatch is decoupled from the aggregate's transaction and delivery guarantees become explicit.
pitfalls: Broadcast is lossy under pressure: a slow receiver returns RecvError::Lagged and misses messages, so events that must not be lost still need a durable log or outbox.
Sending fails when every Receiver has been dropped, and events sent before a consumer subscribes are not replayed, so publish-before-subscribe needs an explicit policy.
